It's Black Friday week and the Apple discounts keep on coming! If you're after a new MacBook, Apple Watch, iPad, or a different piece of Apple gear, then now is the best time to buy, as we're seeing some absolutely killer deals.
Take the always-in-demand MacBook Neo, which has received one of its first major discounts since the price rose to $699 earlier in the year. It's currently available for just $649 at Amazon. If you need a machine with a little more power, then there are also big savings to be had on various MacBook Air and MacBook Pro models.
Deals don't stick around forever, and some are selling out quickly, so act fast if you see something that you like here.
We'll be on hand all day today, November 25, to bring you the best Apple deals we can find, so keep checking back to see what's new.
iPhone 18 Pro: free w/ new line + unlimited @ T-Mobile T-Mobile is offering the iPhone 18 Pro for free when you open a new line and use three T-Mobile Picks. (T-Mobile's new data plans offer up to 3 Picks or free perks, such as DashPass by DoorDash or Netflix Standard. The number of Picks you get is based on the plan's price or how many phone lines are on your plan). In our iPhone 18 Pro review , we said it's the best phone money can buy. The iPhone 18 Pro features a 6.3-inch OLED 120Hz display (2622 x 1206), A20 Pro chipset, and 256GB of storage. You also get a 48MP main, 48MP ultrawide, 48MP telephoto lens w/ 4x zoom, and an 18MP front camera.
In our AirPods Pro 3 review, we said these earbuds are the best AirPods yet. With features like Live Translation, heart rate tracking, and integrated Siri, they're ideal if you want your earbuds to work for you. But if you "just" want industry-leading earbuds with perfect sound and great ANC, the Pro 3 won't let you down.
Price check: $149 @ Walmart | Sold out @ Amazon
Apple Watch Series 12 delivers the line's most accurate heart rate sensing yet, alongside a suite of advanced health and fitness features. It's powered by Apple's new S11 chip, which enables new Audio Intelligence features like Live Rewind and Siri Recap.
I didn't expect to see this deal. The new iPad mini A20 Pro is $100 off. The new model sports a larger 8.5-inch Super Retina XDR Display (2316 x 1512), A20 Pro CPU, 24% smaller bezels than its predecessor, and better audio. You also get a 12MP camera on the front and back and Wi-Fi 7 support. The base models (128GB/256GB) boast a 5-core CPU with 2 super cores and 3 efficiency cores, whereas the 512GB model bumps it to a 6-core CPU with 2 super cores and 4 efficiency cores. This is the first time it's on sale.
The Mac mini M6 keeps the ultra-compact 5x5-inch design introduced with the prior generation, but packs major performance upgrades under the hood. You get the raw speed of Apple's M6 chip, upgraded graphics with hardware-accelerated ray tracing for better 1080p gaming, 16GB of unified memory, and improved connectivity thanks to Apple's custom N1 chip, which adds Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, and Thread support.
Speaking of Apple Watch deals, one of my favorite Apple Watch straps for workouts — the stretchy, breathable, infinitely adjustable Apple Sport Loop — is on sale for 23% off at Walmart ahead of Black Friday in lovely Ultramarine. It fits Apple Watch models with a case size between 44mm and 49mm.
The Apple Watch SE 3 is a great value, even at full price, making it one of the best Apple Watch models for most people. But you can score one right now for a sizable 28% off or just $179 for the 40mm GPS model. That said, I have seen the SE 3 go for even lower; this time last year, it dropped to $149 right around BF. Could the same happen in 2026? Your guess is as good as mine.
Apple's Magic Mouse has a controversial design, but it's still managed to stand the test of time — even making its way into Apple's USB-C era. If you need to pick up one of these for your own Mac, it's on sale now for Black Friday.
The Magic Mouse offers a lightweight and ergonomic design, complete with a long battery life. Not to mention the fact that it also offers basic gestures that will help you control your Mac, and instant pairing to end the pain of needed to go through the awkward Bluetooth setup.
Apple Magic Mouse: was $79 now $59 @ Best Buy
Apple's AirTags are one of the best ways to keep track of your stuff. Whether you put it on your keys, into a bag, or simply want to check your luggage has arrived at the right airport, the AirTag covers it all. All it needs is for another Apple device to pass by and the Find My network will update its location for you.
The second generation AirTags also have the added benefit of louder speakers and improved precision tracking, which helps you track them down more easily.
Apple AirTag: was $29 now $18 @ Amazon Apple AirTag 4-Pack: was $99 now $79 @ Amazon
Apple AirPods Pro 3 are the best earbuds Apple has right now, and while expensive the extra cost is definitely worth it. Personally I will never go back to the awkward EarPod design Apple still employs on the AirPods 5. Thankfully Black Friday has knocked $100 off.
AirPods Pro 3 have some of the best active noise cancelling around, 8 hours of battery life per charge (which rises to 24 hours if you include the case), IP67 water and dust resistance, built-in heart rate sensing, live translation from Apple Intelligence, access to Siri and a bunch more AAI-powered features for you to enjoy.
Apple AirPods Pro 3: was $249 now $149 @ Amazon
If you're looking to save on your next iPhone, then AT&T has you covered. You can pick up the iPhone 18 Pro without paying a penny for the device. All you need to do is trade in an eligible device in good condition, and sign up for an AT&T Premium 2.0 plan or higher for three years.
You'll then receive monthly credits covering the cost of the phone, and means you only need to worry about covering the cost of the data plan itself. The iPhone 18 Pro Max is covered by a similar deal, though the increased cost means you do have to pay the extra $100 yourself.
iPhone 18 Pro: was $1,199 now $0 @ AT&T iPhone 18 Pro Max: was $1,299 now $100 @ AT&T
If you're looking for a large-screen iPad, but don't want the expense of an iPad Pro, there's always the iPad Air. The latest lightweight Apple tablet comes powered by the M4 chipset, which offers excellent performance and energy efficiency — making this a machine that is capable, portable and long-lasting.
The iPad Air has also been discounted for Black Friday, letting you save on the latest Apple purchase.
iPad Air M4 (11-inch): was $749 now $649 @ Best Buy iPad Air M4 (13-inch): was $949 now $849 @ Best Buy
Need a new desktop machine? There are few better options than the latest Mac mini, which is powered by the latest M6 chip. This model comes with 16GB of RAM, a 256GB SSD and two rear USB-C ports. The M6 chip also offers improved graphics and computing power, with a healthy boost to AI processing at the same time.
All while offering the compact design the Mac mini lineup is known for — even if they aren't quite as compact as they were a couple of years ago.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia sellers seek new buyers as U.S. curbs China AI chip access, sources tell CNBC
articles.title_zh: Nvidia sellers seek new buyers as U.S. curbs China AI chip access, sources tell CNBC
articles.content_orig:
Technology stocks plunged on Wednesday as excitement over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's return faded and failed to calm mounting concerns over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped nearly 4%. Semiconductor stocks dragged on the index, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF that tracks the sector plummeted 7%.
After notching one of its best days on record Monday, Nvidia has fallen in the days since and slumped 8% Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices , Micron Technology , Marvell Technology and Intel all dropped more than 9%, with some plunging further.
Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday briefly revived appetite for tech stocks but didn't fully calm investor concerns over the high costs tied to the AI build-out and worries of a potential slowdown.
Other stocks tied to the AI trade also plummeted. Oracle dropped 8% and CoreWeave and Nebius sank more than 10% each.
Wednesday's declines also came as Wall Street digested a hot inflation reading that fueled concerns that higher interest rates could dent demand for growth stocks, including tech.
Amazon , Tesla and Alphabet each declined about 5%. Microsoft lost more than 2% and Meta traded marginally lower.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration to introduce new tariffs on China, EU and 12 other major trading partners
articles.title_zh: Trump administration to introduce new tariffs on China, EU and 12 other major trading partners
articles.content_orig:
The Trump administration said it will issue a new wave of tariffs on China and other major U.S. trading partners, the latest escalation in global trade tensions.
The U.S. will increase tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20%, raising the total tariff rate on the world's second-largest economy to 45%. President Trump also plans to raise taxes on specific products from the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan and India.
Brazil is among the countries that will be hardest hit, with the U.S. planning to raise tariffs on the country's raw and refined sugar and to impose a new 10% levy on aircraft.
The planned tariffs are meant to curtail trade practices that the U.S. says undercut American companies, including what the White House has called excessive manufacturing output from those economies.
"For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market-distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base,"  U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement .
The planned duties would be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which authorizes the USTR to investigate trade agreements if they violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces, or actively discriminate against American goods.
The announcement came after the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR) completed a series of months-long investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and Taiwan. The USTR is also investigating Mexico and Norway but hasn't imposed any new tariffs on those countries.
In a call with reporters late Tuesday, a senior administration official said the tariffs are in the proposal phase and did not provide an implementation timeline. The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted at specific products and would not be stacked on top of existing tariffs introduced by the Trump administration.
Stephen Brown, chief North American economist for Capital Economics, said in a research note Wednesday that the Trump administration's announcement is "not as alarming as it looks." The new tariffs will essentially replace previously announced Section 301 tariffs, rather than stacking on top of them, he said.
Tariffs have been a central part of the Trump administration's economic agenda, with the president arguing they are necessary to boost U.S. manufacturing, create jobs and reduce the trade deficit. However, his authority to impose the levies has faced legal challenges, complicating the rollout.
In February, the Supreme Court blocked a sweeping set of tariffs that the president implemented in 2025 under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, dismantling a key part of the administration's efforts and forcing the government to issue refunds to thousands of affected businesses.
Still, the administration has found other avenues to impose the levies, using other sections of trade law, such as Section 232, which allows the president to restrict imports that could threaten U.S. national security.
The average statutory U.S. tariff rate on imports is now 11.2%, according to the Yale Budget Lab.
The White House moved to propose the new tariffs on Wednesday despite mounting frustration among U.S. voters over rising costs. In a CBS News poll conducted after the midterms, 66% of respondents said President Trump's tariffs have hurt the national economy.
Tariffs are taxes on imported goods. They raise costs for businesses, which sometimes pass the burden onto consumers in the form of higher prices.
We Pay the Tariffs, a grassroots coalition of small businesses, decried the new tariffs, warning they could raise prices just as the holiday season heats up.
"Three weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses," Dan Anthony, executive director of We Pay the Tariffs, said in a statement. "Customers can't afford more price increases, but small businesses can't afford to absorb tariffs on top [of] tariffs either."
The Associated  Press contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: China investigates Shanghai party chief, raising questions over Xi’s succession plans
articles.title_zh: China investigates Shanghai party chief, raising questions over Xi’s succession plans
articles.content_orig:
FILE - Chen Jining, Communist Party Secretary for Shanghai attends a deliberation on the government work report, on the sideline of the National People's Congress at the Beijing Hotel, March 6, 2025. Ng Han Guan/AP hide caption
BANGKOK — Chinese Communist Party authorities are investigating Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining for suspected violations of party discipline, China's anti-corruption watchdog said Tuesday.
The Politburo member is the latest senior official targeted in President Xi Jinping's long-running anti-corruption campaign, which has shown no signs of letting up in scope or depth.
Chen is under investigation by the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The brief announcement by China's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection provided no further details.
A statement released by the Shanghai city government said the Standing Committee of the Shanghai Committee of the CCP "expressed firm support" for the decision to investigate Chen.
The decision sent "a clear and powerful signal that the fight against corruption would continue without pause or retreat," but with "a firm determination to win," the statement said.
The investigation follows sweeping purges under Xi, who has emphasized greater party discipline. The Chinese leader has pursued an anti-corruption campaign for more than a decade, carrying out purges on a scale not seen since Mao Zedong's rule.
"The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping's anti-corruption campaign has no limits," Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, said in an emailed statement. "This is the fourth Politburo member to fall, and the fourth sitting member brought down in the current cycle. The pattern is unprecedented."
The recent Politburo purges highlight how much Chinese politics depend on shifting circumstances, with even officials with qualities that Xi apparently valued being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at American University based in Washington.
"On paper," they appear to be "individuals Xi would appreciate," Torigian said, but afterward, "we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them."
Other Politburo members purged include Gen. Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, both senior members of the Central Military Commission, which oversees the armed forces, and Ma Xingrui, a provincial party secretary.
The post of Shanghai party secretary has traditionally been viewed as a stepping stone to China's top leadership. The country's former President Jiang Zemin, its current premier, Li Qiang, and Xi himself previously held the position.
Chen has served as Shanghai party secretary since 2022. He previously held senior positions in Beijing's municipal government and headed the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

articles.title_orig: US finds no evidence China directed executive to spy on Nvidia CEO, WSJ reports
articles.title_zh: US finds no evidence China directed executive to spy on Nvidia CEO, WSJ reports
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer on Tuesday accused Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang of violating federal laws limiting advanced technology exports to China .
In a post on X, Schumer said Huang "shipped extremely advanced chips to China, violating US export control law, in what amounts to the equivalent of selling rocket engines to the Soviets during the Space Race."
Nvidia and the White House did not immediately comment.
Schumer's statement marked an escalation of congressional criticism against Huang, who was reinstated as chief executive of Nvidia on Monday despite claims regarding his relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese government agent. Lawmakers from both parties are increasingly questioning Nvidia's trade with China, pressing for tighter controls while investigating whether Huang's conduct endangered national security.
Lawmakers have also faulted President Donald Trump for pushing Nvidia to reinstate Huang as CEO.
Schumer and other legislators insist Congress must act rapidly to curtail American chip sales to China. Senator Dave McCormick, a Pennsylvania Republican, said: "Congress must get to the bottom of what happened, and then strengthen our export controls to ensure China can't access our most advanced chips through the back door."
In a separate move on Tuesday, leading Democrats on four House committees wrote to Trump demanding answers about his awareness of Huang’s ties to the suspected agent.
"Your personal relationship with Mr. Huang and your willful blindness to the economic and national security risks posed by this scandal have put the American people at great risk," wrote Representatives Frank Pallone, Gregory Meeks, Jamie Raskin and Robert Garcia, requesting all records of administration contact with the Nvidia board.
"Upon learning that Huang was in a relationship with a suspected agent of the Chinese government, what actions, if any, did Trump take to limit risks to America’s economic and national security?" the lawmakers inquired.
Senator Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, told CNBC on Tuesday that more protections are needed on exports to China. "We might even have to put a babysitter on Jensen Huang," he stated, adding it would be "just to make sure that he doesn't do something that is going to risk the United States."
Huang will appear on December 3 before the US Senate Banking Committee for a public hearing, panel's chair Tim Scott announced Monday.
Huang is also slated for a private briefing on December 1 with three House panels.
Representative Pat Harrigan, a North Carolina Republican, said Huang's "reinstatement today at this juncture is a mistake." He noted: "We sent a signal that one man’s financial impact on our economy outweighs the importance of good governance, good citizenship, and adherence to the law. That is a dangerous precedent to set."

articles.title_orig: Stocks Swoon as AI Fears Spur Rush to Treasuries: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: Stocks Swoon as AI Fears Spur Rush to Treasuries: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Treasury yields fell on Wednesday, with investors fleeing to bonds for protection after October's personal consumption expenditures price index showed that inflation continued to accelerate.
The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 9 basis points lower at 4.809%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which typically moves in line with short-term Federal Reserve interest rate decisions, was down more than 8 basis points at 4.588%.
The longer-dated 30-year Treasury yield, which tends to track geopolitical events, was more than 7 basis points lower at 5.213%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
The personal consumption expenditures price index — the Federal Reserve's preferred gauge of underlying inflation — rose 3.8% year over year for October, in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate. Separately, economic growth came in much stronger for the third quarter. Gross domestic product rose at a 4.3% annualized rate, according to a revised Commerce Department estimate.
The data reinforced expectations for another Fed rate hike in December.
"[I]t is more urgent than ever that Fed officials step up the pace of interest rate hikes to cool off economic demand," said Chris Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. "Rate hikes are coming. Lots of them. Bet on it. The economy and inflation are literally on fire."
Wednesday's drop comes after yields steadied on Tuesday , with traders digesting softer demand for a 5-year Treasury auction.
Trading is shortened this week due to the Thanksgiving holiday. Bond markets will be closed all day Thursday for Thanksgiving, and will close at 2 p.m. E.T. on Friday.
— CNBC's Jeff Cox contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Libyan army vows retaliation after 2 naval officers die of wounds from Ukrainian drone attack
articles.title_zh: Libyan army vows retaliation after 2 naval officers die of wounds from Ukrainian drone attack
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has defended sinking a Russian warship at a Libyan port after one of the country's prominent Western-backed officials accused Kyiv of carrying out "terrorist" attacks and declaring "war" on the North African country.
Ukraine has claimed responsibility for sending naval drones slamming into the Merkury , a Russian corvette, while it sat in the northern Libyan port city of Benghazi early on Sunday.
Dramatic footage showed the seaborne drones hitting the side of the vessel, as Ukraine also said it targeted a military helicopter and a Russian cargo ship carrying weapons for Russia's armed forces.
Russia warned of "very painful consequences" for Ukraine, while Kyiv described the attack as an "exemplary Ukrainian operation."
Ukraine says it has the right to attack Russian assets hundreds of miles away from the frontlines in the east of the country in response to Moscow launching its full-scale invasion of its neighbor nearly five years ago.
But although Kyiv has occasionally hit Russian vessels in the Baltic, Caspian and Mediterranean Seas, the country's long reach—extending far beyond its own borders—has raised fears the grinding war could balloon out further and unsettled even Ukraine's staunch allies. Benghazi is more than 1,000 miles from the trenches of southern Ukraine.
Musa Al-Koni, the vice-president of Libya's Presidential Council in Tripoli, said the attack on the Russian warship was "a declaration of war against the Libyan state," and said authorities in the country "hold the Ukrainian side fully responsible for these terrorist acts."
The North African country is still divided following its civil war, split between the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity—backed by the United Nations—and the military-led eastern administration. The presidential council acts as the head of state.
Rival Libyan authorities in the east of the country, which are generally aligned with the Kremlin, said two Libyan naval officers had been killed in the attack.
Al-Koni said he would refer the matter to the U.N. Security Council and the International Court of Justice in The Hague, which act as the U.N.'s judicial arm.
Ukraine's top diplomat, Andrii Sybiha, said Ukraine was "not 'dragging' anyone into the war or 'transferring' the war anywhere," while a Ukrainian foreign ministry spokesperson said the attack on the Merkury was justified under the United Nations' founding charter, which says each state has the right to self-defense after an armed attack.
"Russia systematically uses its military presence and logistical infrastructure outside its own territory, particularly in Africa, to support military operations and build up capabilities that sustain its war," the spokesperson said.
Russia has leaned more heavily on bases in Libya after scaling down its use of Syrian facilities following the fall of the country's former dictator, Kremlin-aligned Bashar al-Assad, in December 2024.
Moscow has deepened its involvement in swathes of Africa in recent years, including by using its Africa Corps—the successor to the now-disbanded Wagner Group of mercenaries that were influential in the early years of the full-scale war in Ukraine.
A small number of Ukrainian special forces soldiers are reported to have been based in at least two Libyan sites to help carry out attacks on Russian vessels in Libya since late 2025.
The guided-missile Merkury , which has only been in service since 2023, was en route back to Russia, according to officials from Libya's eastern government . It was described as stopping in Libya to refuel and bring on board fresh supplies.
Italy's government, which has largely backed Ukraine despite its right-wing leadership, called the operation a "mistake" and said it had violated Libya's sovereignty.
Meanwhile, Zelensky confirmed on Tuesday that Kyiv was behind an attack on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday.
The Sparta II was traveling from St Petersburg to Russia's Baltic Sea exclave of Kaliningrad when drones smashed into the vessel, prompting all crew members to be evacuated. The vessel was later towed into Russian waters after drifting, ablaze, into Finland's territorial waters.
Finland shares more than 800 miles of border with Russia and has been a vocal advocate for Ukraine as one of NATO's newest members.
But Finland's prime minister, Petteri Orpo, said war was "spilling over into our immediate vicinity," while the country's defense minister said Helsinki had made it clear to Kyiv there were safety and environmental risks involved in targeting Russian assets near civilian shipping routes.

articles.title_orig: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
articles.title_zh: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and President Trump speak to reporters aboard Air Force One. Photo: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images
The Trump administration proposed a new round of tariffs targeting China, the European Union and 12 other economies over policies it says have created excess industrial capacity.
Why it matters: Trump officials are pressing ahead with his trade agenda despite a Democratic midterm sweep fueled by affordability concerns.
Driving the news: The tariffs are the result of  a trade investigation that launched in March , The proposed tariffs are a narrower approach than the sweeping import levies the administration has previously imposed, a senior U.S. official said.
Between the lines: The administration proposed tariffs of up to 20% to 35% on other targeted economies, though lower rates apply to trading partners with deals in place.
The big picture: The investigation was conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration contends that foreign industrial policies encourage companies to produce more goods than global demand can absorb, undercutting U.S. manufacturers.
What they're saying: In response to reports of the proposed tariffs , China dismissed U.S. claims of industrial overcapacity as a "false proposition" and urged Washington to preserve stable trade relations.
Of note: The U.S. is also proposing tougher trade measures against Brazil, after imposing 25% tariffs in July over alleged unfair trade practices amid tensions between Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The bottom line: Trump's tariff agenda is moving forward as Democrats in the incoming Congress look to curb presidential authority over trade policy and lower Americans' costs .
Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

articles.title_orig: Young Britons’ sex lives have fallen off a cliff, major survey shows
articles.title_zh: Young Britons’ sex lives have fallen off a cliff, major survey shows
articles.content_orig:
Young Britons are having half as much sex as they were in 1990, according to a new study, with the average reported frequency falling from four times a month to just twice a month.
The data was produced as part of a long-running study known as the National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal), according to a statement Wednesday from the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), which participates in the research.
“The sex lives of people in Britain have changed markedly since 1990 and they have substantial and varied sexual and reproductive health needs,” LSHTM said.
Researchers randomly selected around 6,700 people from England, Scotland and Wales aged 16-59 to participate in interviews and online surveys between September 2022 and January 2024.
This is the fourth edition of “one of the largest studies of sexual behaviour in the world,” which has previously been undertaken in 1990, 2000 and 2010.
In addition to adults under 45 years old reporting that they are having sex half as much as their peers did in 1990, the survey showed that 77% of 16-59-year-olds reported having sex in the past year, and 89% said they had sex at least once in their lives.
Among 16-24-year-olds, one in three said they had never had sex, up from around one in five in 2010.
Half of young women reported watching pornography in the past 12 months, compared with nearly 90% of male respondents. This was the first time the survey had asked about the use of online pornography.
Attitudes toward children and contraception are also changing. While the use of hormonal contraception declined among young women, the proportion of women who report that they don’t want children has doubled in the past decade.
The survey also reveals important findings for preventing the spread of sexually transmitted infections (STIs), with more than one in four sexually experienced 16-24-year-olds with exclusively opposite-sex partners reporting behaviors that are associated with STI risk.
These include “having four or more partners or condomless sex with two or more partners in the past year or overlapping partners in the past five years,” the statement said.
Men’s sexual health can predict heart issues
“While most adults are having sex, people are having sex less often and more young people have never had sex,” Soazig Clifton, academic director for Natsal at University College London, which also participates in the survey, said in the statement.
“There is also a higher proportion of people reporting same-sex experiences, and online sexual activity is now part of everyday life for many.”
Dr Otilia Mårdh, a scientific officer at the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), who was not involved in the research, said that “another notable Natsal-4 finding is, that the proportion of men reporting both same-sex and opposite-sex partners (MSWM) more than doubled, from 0.9% (Natsal-3) to 2.3%.”
Feeling like a late bloomer when it comes to sex? There’s hope
“The authors note that this growing population could increasingly bridge sexual networks with different STI risks,” Mårdh said in a comment published by the Science Media Centre on Wednesday.
She added that this is “particularly relevant” as surveillance data from European monitoring programs shows “recent increases in syphilis and gonorrhoea among heterosexual populations, alongside rising congenital syphilis — contrasting with historically lower levels.”
“These trends highlight the need for accessible, stigma-free sexual health services offering prevention and testing tailored to people’s needs,” said Mårdh.
Five papers drawing on the results of the survey were published in the journal The Lancet.

China Southern Airlines said in a filing late Tuesday that its subsidiary Xiamen Airlines had agreed to purchase 50 Boeing 737-8 aircraft with a combined catalog price of approximately $7.4 billion.
The announcement comes after President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday that he expected China to purchase another 250 Boeing aircraft, following his meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC summit last week.
"By the way, I sold 250 Boeings to China, and I think they're going to do another 250," Trump said.
In May, China approved an initial purchase of 200 Boeing aircraft for Chinese airlines following Trump's visit to Beijing, marking the country's first commitment to purchase U.S.-made Boeing aircraft since 2017, according to the White House.
It was not immediately clear whether Xiamen Airlines' latest purchase was part of that commitment.
China Southern, which owns a 55% stake in Xiamen Airlines, said the actual purchase price would be lower than the combined list price because of discounts offered by Boeing. The company did not disclose the final purchase price, citing confidentiality provisions in the agreement.
The aircraft are scheduled to be delivered in batches between 2031 and 2034, with the purchase financed through a combination of internal funds and external financing, the filing showed. The transaction remains subject to shareholder and relevant Chinese government approvals.
China Southern said the purchase would support Xiamen Airlines' planned relocation to the new Xiamen Xiang'an International Airport and the expansion of its route network.
The agreement follows the group's recent purchase agreement for 137 Airbus A320neo - family aircraft, the filing showed. China Southern said sourcing aircraft from different manufacturers would help diversify its fleet and improve operational flexibility.
Other Asian carriers, including Philippine Airlines and Malaysia Aviation Group , have also announced Boeing aircraft orders this month.

articles.title_orig: Poland Asks NATO to Shoot Down Russian Missiles Over Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Poland Asks NATO to Shoot Down Russian Missiles Over Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
The drone was not shot down as it "changed course to head east," Warsaw said.
LONDON -- A Russian drone violated Polish airspace late on Monday night during Moscow's latest wave of long-range strikes on Ukraine, the Polish military said, in a week that has seen multiple incidents related to the four-year-old conflict reported in theaters far from the frontline.
Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 96 drones, of which 64 were jet-powered, into the country overnight. Air defenders downed or suppressed 73 drones, of which 45 were jet-powered, the air force said. Impacts were reported across 13 locations.
Poland's Armed Forces Operational Command said in a post to X that "a Russian unmanned aerial vehicle briefly violated Polish airspace" during the overnight attacks while targeting western Ukraine.
The command said it "activated the necessary air defense forces and assets" and gave permission for the drone to be shot down. "The object was continuously tracked by military radar systems throughout its flight path," the command said.
"After the unmanned aerial vehicle changed course to head east, taking into account the potential threat to civilians and the possible consequences of shooting down the object, a decision was made to refrain from using weapons due to the continuing risk of causing damage," the command said.
Russian missiles and drones have violated Polish airspace multiple times since the start of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Elsewhere, NATO allies have reported confirmed or suspected Russian drone violations in Romania, Lithuania and Latvia. Russian drones have also been discovered in Moldova, which is not a NATO member. Russian officials have denied responsibility for all such incursions.
The most notable recent example saw three Russian cruise missiles land on Polish territory during attacks on Ukraine earlier this month. The incident prompted an emergency meeting of NATO members on Monday, with the alliance agreeing to deploy an AWACS early-warning aircraft deployment to Poland.
On Tuesday, Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said Polish officials were due to meet on several security issues including "protecting Polish airspace, violations of our airspace, NATO support -- early warning aircraft and a permanent U.S. military base in Poland."
As the war approaches its five-year anniversary, its ripples have spread far beyond southern and eastern Ukraine, where the fighting is concentrated.
This week, for example, Ukraine claimed naval drone attacks on a Russian warship and a cargo vessel in the Libyan port of Benghazi.
Also this week, authorities and analysts reported two drone attacks on Russian cargo ships in the Baltic Sea.

Technology stocks plunged on Wednesday as excitement over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang 's return faded and failed to calm mounting concerns over the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped nearly 4%. Semiconductor stocks dragged on the index, and the VanEck Semiconductor ETF that tracks the sector plummeted 7%.
After notching one of its best days on record Monday, Nvidia has fallen in the days since and slumped 8% Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices , Micron Technology , Marvell Technology and Intel all dropped more than 9%, with some plunging further.
Huang's return to Nvidia on Monday briefly revived appetite for tech stocks but didn't fully calm investor concerns over the high costs tied to the AI build-out and worries of a potential slowdown.
Other stocks tied to the AI trade also plummeted. Oracle dropped 8% and CoreWeave and Nebius sank more than 10% each.
Wednesday's declines also came as Wall Street digested a hot inflation reading that fueled concerns that higher interest rates could dent demand for growth stocks, including tech.
Amazon , Tesla and Alphabet each declined about 5%. Microsoft lost more than 2% and Meta traded marginally lower.

Nvidia ( NVDA ) stock retreated another 8% on Wednesday, following a 6% decline in the prior session as chip stocks continued to plunge amid a broader market sell-off.
Peers AMD ( AMD ) and Broadcom ( AVGO ) also extended losses from the prior session.
This year's once-hot AI trades continue to tumble, with memory chipmaker Micron Technology ( MU ) and peer SK Hynix ( SKHY ) tanking 11% and 8% respectively. Micron is more than 50% off its all-time high over the summer.
Storage and memory players Seagate (STX ), Western Digital ( WDC ), and Sandisk ( SNDK ) all fell on Wednesday. Sandisk, which recently implemented a stock split, is down roughly 70% from its June record high.
The violent move follows a stunning rally on Monday when Nvidia jumped 31% after the AI chip giant's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. But some strategists say tighter financial conditions and lingering questions around the AI trade are weighing on sentiment.
"There is still a lot of nervousness out there, and some investors have taken advantage of Monday's jump to cut their exposure to the AI trade," said David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation, on Wednesday.
He also noted the prevailing view that Huang is the only person who can hold the AI trade together "reeks of desperation," while investors increasingly perceive that "Nvidia's board is not the one that the world's leading chip designer should want."
Other areas of the AI trade retreated on Wednesday, including the stocks of neocloud providers CoreWeave ( CRWV ) and Nebius ( NBIS ), which each dropped by double-digit percentages.

articles.title_zh: Migrant arrivals in Spain's Canary Islands break single-day record
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Spanish authorities confirmed that almost 2,000 migrants reached Spain ’s Canary Islands on Tuesday, setting a record high for arrivals across the archipelago in a single day.
Situated off the West African coast, the islands experienced this surge in arrivals just before Spain holds a national election later this week, when migration will be a major concern for voters.
Spain’s maritime rescue service reported that 1,990 people landed aboard 15 separate boats as rescue vessels escorted one dinghy after another into the small island of El Hierro.
"Sadly, this is a historic day," the Canary Islands' regional leader Fernando Clavijo said in an interview with Spanish radio station Cadena Ser.
Around 100 minors were among Tuesday’s arrivals, including a four-day-old baby born during the ocean journey, Clavijo said.
The Canary Islands, a tourist hotspot for many Europeans drawn to year-round mild weather, have for years been a key entry point for migrants desperate to reach Europe. The route is extremely dangerous, with thousands dying in the attempted crossing.
Although the islands lie about 65 miles (105 kilometres) from the nearest African coast, many migrants take longer routes to evade security forces. Journeys can last days or weeks, with many boats missing their target and drifting into the open Atlantic.
More than 26,000 people have reached the Canary Islands this year, with half that total arriving in November. The previous single-day record occurred just two weeks earlier, when 1,400 people reached Gran Canaria on 7 November.
In June, Pope Leo warned people smugglers that they will face God’s wrath for exploiting the desperation of migrants when the pontiff visited the islands.
Departures from West Africa are seasonal, and November often sees spikes in numbers as many leave before ocean waters become rough during winter. Calm seas recently have contributed to the high number of departures.
Most boats arriving on Tuesday originated from Senegal and Gambia, Clavijo said. Despite European Union efforts in West Africa to reduce migrant numbers, many believe leaving is their only option to find work and build a better life.
"The sailing conditions were favorable and there was a full moon, so these people looking for a better future ended up on our shores," Clavijo said.
Clavijo stated that El Hierro, the westernmost member of the archipelago with a population of 12,000, could not handle such a large influx of people, many of whom arrived exhausted and in poor condition.
He said he was satisfied overall with the transfer of adult migrants to mainland Spain, but requested help from other regions to take in unaccompanied minors who need to be cared for by authorities.
Migration promises to be a main issue for Spain's election.
Spain’s conservative Popular Party is aiming to unseat the ruling Socialist-led central government in Sunday’s elections. To do so, it would likely have to form a government with the far-right Vox party, which is campaigning heavily on expelling migrants and social policies that favour Spaniards over recent arrivals.
Without mentioning Vox, Clavijo, who belongs to the regional Canary Coalition party, denounced any attempts to demonise migrants, calling it "a xenophobic discourse of bad people."
The Canary Island leader also slammed the recent deal by Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands to send migrants to Rwanda, calling it "ridiculous."
"Europe is on the wrong path," Clavijo said.

articles.title_orig: Inside Trump's effort to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO
articles.title_zh: Inside Trump's effort to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
WASHINGTON — In May 2017, just months into his first term, President Trump welcomed Russians into the Oval Office . At that meeting, he disclosed highly classified intelligence collected by Israeli partners that risked compromising a coveted allied source.
He went on in the years to come to resist security protocols around his personal communications, plowing through the clearance process for his close aides and family. He shared classified reconnaissance imagery on Twitter. He removed some of the most sensitive secrets in the U.S. government after leaving office, storing them in a bathroom at Mar-a-Lago , and at an event there openly discussed the whereabouts of U.S. nuclear submarines.
Now, the president is once again under fire for dismissing counterintelligence concerns, this time over a Chinese espionage campaign targeting Nvidia , the world’s largest AI chipmaker and one of the nation’s most valuable companies.
This week, Trump succeeded in persuading Nvidia’s board to reinstate Jensen Huang as its leader, despite his admission to engaging in an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The president cited the stock market’s reaction to Huang’s firing as one of his leading motivations.
Criticism came from across the Republican spectrum, from the party’s old guard to some of Trump’s most loyal supporters.
“I would have hoped the president had other tools for stimulating the AI-driven stock market than rewarding Chinese high-tech espionage,” said John D. Woodward Jr., a former CIA officer and senior Defense Department official now at Boston University.
Intelligence officials sounded an alarm last year over the Huang affair, raising concern at the CIA and prompting Marco Rubio, the national security advisor and secretary of state, to issue a warning to Trump. The president requested more information, but chose not to act after a preliminary review failed to identify a smoking gun that Huang had passed valuable information to the mistress, officials said.
Still, intelligence officials told lawmakers this week that Huang’s love interest, named Alice Huang, did in fact pass information to Chinese officials while the affair was ongoing.
Alice Huang had been a top executive at Megaspeed International, a Singapore-based firm accused of purchasing advanced Nvidia chips to then siphon to China, bypassing U.S. export restrictions.
Advanced computer chips are the core of a competition between the United States and China as the dueling superpowers sprint for supremacy in artificial intelligence.
Trump has repeatedly said there is no acceptable alternative to an American victory in that race. But concern has grown across party lines that Trump has grown reticent to confront China over its espionage attempts targeting U.S. companies at the technological frontier.
“Let me get this straight,” Mitt Romney, a former Republican senator from Utah and the 2012 GOP presidential nominee, wrote on social media this week. “We rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they’d need to get ahead of us.”
“Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse,” he added.
But Trump has been dismissive of intelligence concerns before.
Throughout his first term, Trump repeatedly rejected the unanimous assessment of U.S. intelligence agencies that Russia had interfered in the 2016 election to help him win. Most notoriously, at a 2018 news conference in Helsinki alongside Vladimir Putin, Trump said he trusted the Russian president’s word over the conclusions of his own intelligence community.
“My people came to me, Dan Coats came to me and some others, they said they think it’s Russia,” Trump said at the time, referring to his director of national intelligence. “I have President Putin — he just said it’s not Russia. I will say this: I don’t see any reason why it would be.”
“So I have great confidence in my intelligence people,” he added, “but I will tell you that President Putin was extremely strong and powerful in his denial today.”
Last spring, on his first of two visits to China this year, Trump told reporters that espionage from Beijing did not concern him.
“They’re talking about the spying. Well, we do it too,” Trump said aboard Air Force One, shortly after White House staff threw burner phones off the plane before takeoff. “We spy like hell on them, too.”
In an interview with CNBC on Monday, Trump said that the Nvidia co-founder and chief executive has been “exonerated” in a preliminary “study” of the episode. Huang did not pose a threat to national security by leading the company, Trump told the board.
“They did ask for assurance on the national security threat, and we gave them assurance, at least with everything we know,” Trump said, “and we know a lot.
“He’s apologized for indiscretion, which was unfortunate,” he added. “That was probably — that’s what brought it to such a level. Because sex sells, fellas!”

articles.title_orig: How To Unlock Hurricane Weather In ‘GTA 6’
articles.title_zh: How To Unlock Hurricane Weather In ‘GTA 6’
articles.content_orig:
Grand Theft Auto 6 GTA 6 Rockstar Games
Grand Theft Auto 6 is a massive world filled with an incredible amount of detail and simulation. This includes the game’s dynamic and realistic weather system, a feature Rockstar hyped up quite a bit before launch. However, some players online aren’t seeing much rain and are claiming Rockstar lied. The reality is that, yes, rainstorms happen, but you might not be seeing them very often for a few reasons.
If you search around Reddit or Twitter , you’ll see a lot of people complaining that it never rains in GTA 6. However, you can also find amazing clips of thunderstorms pummeling Vice City. And I can confirm that when I played GTA 6 pre-release, I saw rainstorms and other weather events, like fog.  So what’s going on here? Why are some people suggesting the weather system in GTA 6 isn’t working or was a lie, while others, like myself, are dealing with thunderstorms?
THIS ISN'T JUST RAIN. THIS IS ENVIRONMENTAL ARTISTRY AT AN ABSURD LEVEL! 🤯
Just look at the rain dripping off the sides of the bridge, the incredibly atmospheric overcast skies and the way the entire scene comes together. GTA 6 genuinely looks like a work of art!
I'm quite… pic.twitter.com/NjbjmeYHV7
— VideoGameDetails (@VideoGameDetail) November 24, 2026
First up is that it does seem like something was borked with GTA 6 ‘s dynamic weather system at launch. On Monday, the first post-launch patch for GTA 6 arrived and fixed an issue that, according to Rockstar’s patch notes, led to the weather not changing for extended periods of time. So yeah, one reason it might not have been raining in your game is because of a bug.
However, even after the patch, some people are still claiming it isn’t raining in GTA 6 . And maybe something is still bugged. The more likely explanation is that people don’t realize just how dynamic and advanced the weather is in GTA 6.
In all previous Grand Theft Auto games and most other open-world games, when it rains in the game, it rains across the whole map. That’s not how weather in GTA 6 works. Instead, storms, fog, and other weather events can happen locally and in small parts of the map. At one point I was flying a plane and it was sunny, but ahead in the sky were big dark clouds. As I reached them, I entered a rainstorm. As I left the clouds behind, the rain stopped. So it’s very possible that it is raining somewhere in your GTA 6 world; you just aren’t in the spot where the rain is falling.
I’ve also seen some people suggesting the weather is locked to certain conditions earlier in the game, which seems plausible but hasn’t been confirmed by Rockstar yet. Once I reached chapter three of the game, I had a few in-game days when it rained a lot. I started to miss the sun.
The point is that, no, Rockstar didn’t lie. Grand Theft Auto 6 ‘s dynamic weather system is so good that I think some people are just dodging the rain without realizing it. The size of the map and the randomness at play in the system may mean that you go for a while without encountering rainy weather, but keep playing and sooner or later, the storms will come.

articles.title_orig: Fed's preferred gauge of inflation climbs ahead of possible rate hike - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Fed's preferred gauge of inflation climbs ahead of possible rate hike - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The Fed will issue a decision on interest rates early next month.
The Federal Reserve's preferred gauge of inflation climbed in October, according to a government report issued on Wednesday. The measure is sure to draw attention from central bankers as they weigh a possible rate increase early next month.
The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index (PCE) showed annual inflation climbed from 3.6% in September to 3.8% in October. The reading matched economists' expectations.
That figure for October marked the highest annual PCE in five months, putting inflation nearly two percentage points above the Fed's target level of 2%.
The report arrived weeks after a separate inflation measure, the Consumer Price Index (CPI), showed a larger jump in prices in October than economists had expected.
Fuel prices have accounted for a sizable share of overall inflation since the outbreak of the Iran war in late February set off a global oil supply shortage.
A cooldown in oil prices since the midterm elections has put downward pressure on gasoline prices, however, leaving the national average price of a gallon of gas at $3.58 as of Wednesday, AAA data showed. That figure amounted to a decline of about 15% from a month earlier.
The relief at the pump in recent weeks did not appear in the report on Wednesday, since it detailed prices in October.
The fresh data is sure to garner attention from the Fed at a delicate moment, when policymakers are weighing a rate increase that could help tackle inflation but risks a slowdown in hiring.
A stronger-than-expected jobs report earlier this month may ease possible concern among central bankers about a cooldown for the labor market.
Economic growth has also proven resilient, displaying better-than-expected performance in a quarterly report on gross domestic product released last month.
If the Fed were to issue a rate increase at its next meeting in December, the decision would mark the central bank's second rate hike in four months, after it had gone three years without raising rates.
The odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's next meeting are pegged at about 97%, according to CME Group's FedWatch Tool , a measure of market sentiment.
Days before the midterm elections, Fed policymakers opted to hold interest rates steady as they awaited further economic data. Still, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh vowed to cool off inflation.
"It’s our responsibility to get inflation down," Warsh said at a press conference in Washington, D.C., at the time.
Wall Street will also take notice of the PCE report after a volatile stretch of trading. The major stock indexes were mixed on Tuesday after soaring a day earlier in response to an announcement from Nvidia reinstating Jensen Huang as CEO.
Those fluctuations followed a selloff last week as tech investors digested fallout from Huang's previous resignation as well as an initial public offering from artificial intelligence giant Anthropic.

articles.title_orig: U.S. economy grew at rapid 4.3% pace in third quarter, new estimate shows
articles.title_zh: U.S. economy grew at rapid 4.3% pace in third quarter, new estimate shows
articles.content_orig:
The US economy boomed last quarter, growing at an annualized rate of 4.3%, the Commerce Department reported on Wednesday. That’s a massive jump from the 3.4% rate initially reported. Both figures take inflation into account.
Business investment, boosted by software spending, was the single biggest driver of the third-quarter surge, a sign of major AI-related spending. Consumer spending, which accounts for three quarters of gross domestic product, also played a key role in delivering the best quarter of economic growth in three years.
But that robust growth comes with an inflation complication. In separate data released Wednesday, the Personal Consumption Expenditures price index — the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge — showed prices accelerated slightly to an annualized rate of 3.8% in October from 3.7% the prior month. That’s almost double the Fed’s target of 2%, solidifying the case for a rate hike next month.
On a monthly basis, price increases slowed to 0.3% from 0.5% in September.
The booming economy isn’t translating into increased wealth for many Americans, whose savings have dwindled as income growth has slowed.
While Wednesday’s PCE report showed that the personal savings rate (savings as a percentage of after-tax income) rose 0.5 percentage points to 4.1%, it’s below the 4.9% rate seen in October of last year. The increase in savings came from a boost in after-tax income growth last month, though much of that was tied to Medicare rebate payments.
But in a potentially worrisome sign for the economy, Americans are reining in their spending: When stripping out the 0.3% monthly price increase, spending was flat for October.
“The cautious consumer is back. It will be a bargain-hunting holiday for many Americans,” Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, wrote in a note Wednesday.
CNN’s Alicia Wallace contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s Eisenkot secures first coalition partner in bid to form government
articles.title_zh: Israel’s Eisenkot secures first coalition partner in bid to form government
articles.content_orig:
The party of Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has announced an agreement to unite with a right-wing party in a bid to form the next government following October’s elections .
The centrist Yashar party said on Tuesday that it agreed to sign a coalition pact with Israel Our Home party after a meeting with its leader Avigdor Lieberman, the first alliance of its kind since the election.
After no bloc managed to secure a 61-seat majority, Israel’s parliament was sworn in on November 10 without a new government.
President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming ⁠a government, while Likud party leader Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister despite the October 27 election stripping him of his majority.
Eisenkot has until December 6 to form a government under a 28-day mandate, though he could ask for a 14-day extension. If Eisenkot fails, Netanyahu would have an opportunity to do so. If no one is able to form a government, another election will be held next year.
The right-wing Likud’s alliance with far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties holds 53 of the Knesset’s 120 seats.
Eisenkot’s centre-right Yashar party and patchwork coalition partners, including Lieberman, hold 48 seats. But they have potential allies in the parties representing Israel’s Palestinian minority, which hold 19 seats and ⁠are aligned with Eisenkot in their vehement opposition to Netanyahu.
Lieberman had once served as foreign minister under a previous Netanyahu government but has since become a strong critic.
Talks are also ongoing between Eisenkot, some of his “change bloc” partners and Likud on forming a unity government.
The left-wing Democrats party, which won eight parliament seats, separately said it was suspending talks with Eisenkot after the Yashar party leader’s talks with Netanyahu’s Likud on a possible unity government.
Yair Golan, head of the Democrats, said he prefers a government without Netanyahu but with the Arab parties.

articles.title_orig: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the Ukraine war, new estimate suggests
articles.title_zh: More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in the Ukraine war, new estimate suggests
articles.content_orig:
More than 700,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in Ukraine , according to a new projection based on leaked official data, an estimate that sheds new light on the staggering cost of President Vladimir Putin ’s war.
The grim assessment comes more than 4½ years after the Kremlin’s invasion of its neighbor, an all-out war that has consumed Russian society . The death toll has been mounting with each painstaking ground assault, with no end to the conflict in sight despite pressure from President Donald Trump for Kyiv to make a deal.
The leak from Russia’s state statistics agency, Rosstat — released by Belarusian and Ukrainian hackers earlier this month — reveals that at least 490,000 Russian soldiers had been killed in Ukraine based on registered deaths as of the end of September. That’s according to breakdowns by a range of independent media, including the BBC and others, that were published this week. But one exiled Russian media outlet, Meduza, also used the leaked mortality data to project the total number of military deaths, including those that have not yet been recorded.
Meduza estimates that number to be 720,000.
NBC News did not have access to the leaked data and could not authenticate it or independently confirm these numbers.
Neither Moscow nor Kyiv provide regular updates on their battlefield losses.
Mediazona, along with the BBC Russian Service and a team of volunteers, has been compiling a separate named list of Russian war dead using open-source data for years, given the difficulty of gauging the true impact of the war on Russian society.
In its analysis, Mediazona said it arrived at the 490,000 war dead number from the 29.7 million records it obtained from the hackers that covered nearly all death registrations in Russia from early 2021 through September this year, based mainly on records with an “explicit military cause of death” and court rulings declaring people dead.
The leaked data was cross-checked against Mediazona’s own named list and matched 95% of the records, as well as the publicly accessible national Probate Registry, a database of inheritance cases, and Rosstat’s own official mortality statistics, the outlet said.
Mediazona said it also checked against possible data tempering and fake military death injections by cross-referencing a unique vital record number that every death registration carries, and court rulings, which often cite death record numbers.
“We are confident that this data is genuine,” the outlet said, adding that fabricating a dataset of this scale from scratch would be “impossible” especially as it checks out against official registries.
The hackers shared leaked data with a number of other exiled Russian media outlets and the BBC, who all arrived at a figure close to the 490,000 reported by Mediazona. A similar estimate of half a million Russian troops killed was also shared by a senior British defense official in September.
Before the new analysis of the data in the Rosstat leak, the verified named list of Russia’s war dead compiled by Mediazona and the BBC stood at just over 289,000. It was based on obituaries, local news and official registries, and was the only publicly available database containing the fallen soldiers’ names.
The Russian Defense Ministry has not officially updated its death toll in Ukraine since the early months of the war, when then-Defense Minister Sergei Shoigu said it stood at nearly 6,000.
Mediazona warned that due to a considerable lag in military death registrations, Rosstat may not yet have finished capturing deaths from 2025. “That means the leaked records through late September — however authentic and reliable they are — still fall short of the true death toll,” it said.
It was this that prompted Meduza to try and calculate an estimate of total Russian losses to date — 720,000 people, a figure that includes deaths it predicts will be registered later.
“Since 2024, the share of late registrations has grown dramatically, and it continues to rise,” the outlet said in its own analysis, adding that the 2026 data is extremely incomplete for both missing service members and other military deaths. It said it used epidemiology and tools like the “chain-ladder method” from actuarial science, which uses mathematics to help measure the probability and risk of future events, to arrive at the projected estimate. These methods allowed Meduza to calculate the number of military deaths that it estimates have happened but haven’t yet shown up in the data, the outlet said.
“Today, it’s simply impossible to leave this category out of an overall estimate of the dead,” it added.
The Kremlin dismissed the analysis Wednesday.
“The only department authorized to officially release data on casualties is the Ministry of Defense of the Russian Federation,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov told NBC News during a call with reporters, when asked if the Kremlin was aware of the 700,000 projected estimate by Meduza.
“I suggest disregarding any other data,” he added.
It is similarly difficult to ascertain the true number of Ukrainian soldiers killed fighting against Russia. Kyiv has been slightly more forthcoming, with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy volunteering some estimates of battlefield losses in recent years, the latest in July putting the total at around 50,000 killed.
But analysts say this is likely an undercount.
An assessment by the Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies earlier this year said up to 150,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed, based on estimates from Britain’s military, Mediazona’s named war dead list, its own estimates and interviews with U.S., European, Ukrainian and other government officials.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
articles.title_zh: U.S. plans to hike tariffs on China, EU, Brazil and others over subsidized production
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump's administration is getting ready to raise tariffs on China, the European Union and a dozen other trading partners
WASHINGTON -- President Donald Trump's administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20% and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.
The new tariffs are meant to discourage excessive manufacturing output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.
In a late-night call with reporters on Tuesday, a senior administration official provided details of the planned tariffs ahead of the release of a series of investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU and the self-governing island of Taiwan. The official insisted on anonymity as a condition for discussing the reports before they were posted by the U.S. Trade Representative's office.
The official stressed that the tariffs were still at the proposal stage and did not provide strict timelines on possible implementation.
The tariffs — rolled out early Wednesday, the day before Thanksgiving — represent another controversial twist in Trump's economic policy. Voters in this month's midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats, with about two-thirds of voters saying that Trump's policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll , a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.
Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year's tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.
The Trump administration argues that these countries have helped spur an influx of goods at lower prices that undercut American companies, creating a trade deficit in goods that has recently exceeded $1 trillion annually.
The legal basis of the planned tariffs is Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which enables the U.S. government to investigate and retaliate against foreign trade practices that violate existing deals, are not justified by market forces or actively discriminate against American goods. The official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes .
Brazil was singled out for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled, the official said. The U.S. is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.
For some Chinese goods, the new 20% tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45%.
The U.S. and China reached a trade truce last year that is set to expire on Jan. 10. The new tariffs will not come as a surprise to Beijing and are unlikely to undermine the truce, the administration official said.
Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China's purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.
The official stressed that the tariffs are targeted to specific products. They would not stack on top of separate tariffs on automobiles, steel, aluminum and other products that the administration has separately imposed under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962.
Neither will they stack on top of levies of 10% to 12.5% announced in July for 60 trading partners that the White House said have inadequately enforced bans on goods produced by forced labor.
Other nations facing the new tariffs are Bangladesh, Cambodia, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Thailand and Vietnam. The official said there are two other countries with pending investigations: Mexico and Norway.
The Associated Press confirmed the planned tariff announcement ahead of the call, according to people who insisted on anonymity because they were not authorized to comment publicly. The plans were reported earlier on Tuesday by Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal.

articles.title_orig: Even the price of toys is on the rise. How Americans are scaling back holiday plans
articles.title_zh: Even the price of toys is on the rise. How Americans are scaling back holiday plans
articles.content_orig:
As Amanda Brecht planned how her family would spend Thanksgiving this year, she had to make some difficult decisions.
Because of high gas prices , the 30-year-old decided she wouldn't drive across her home state of Michigan to celebrate with extended family. Instead, Brecht and her husband will spend the holiday with just their three kids. And with food prices rising, they'll be skipping appetizers and serving turkey breast instead of a whole bird.
"Thanksgiving is definitely going to look different this year," Brecht said. "Money doesn't grow on trees. You can only do so much."
With inflation accelerating, Americans like Brecht will see higher prices almost everywhere they look this holiday season . At a time of year synonymous with food, gifts and big spending, many consumers are instead pinching pennies, paring back their plans and making tough choices about how they'll celebrate.
Some are raiding their savings accounts and running up debt on credit cards. They're reporting downbeat outlooks about the economy in surveys. And they've become more selective with spending as inflationary pressures mount.
"Families are facing some tough choices this year," said Alexander Smith, an associate professor who researches behavioral economics at the Worcester Polytechnic Institute. "They might have to cut back on holiday spending in whatever way that they can."
A classic Thanksgiving feast will be harder to pull off as grocery prices rise.
The price of a 10-person Thanksgiving dinner increased 6% to $58.63 in 2026, according to an annual survey from the American Farm Bureau Federation. Faith Parum, the organization's deputy chief economist, said the price increase was a result of higher costs for labor and transportation.
Grocers including Walmart and Aldi have gained traction on social media by offering Thanksgiving meal bundles as a value-focused workaround to higher prices. Walmart's offering promises to feed 10 for $35, and includes a turkey and ingredients to make mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, cranberries, marshmallow-topped sweet potatoes and a pumpkin pie.
Still, some consumers will feel disappointed by having less choice in their menus due to higher prices, according to Joe Bruseulas, chief economist at tax firm RSM.
"We're missing the point here if all we're doing is focusing on the fact that Walmart will sell you a homogeneous dinner meal" at a discount, Bruseulas said. "People feel horrible that they have to go to that because the price of everything has just risen so significantly over the past five years."
Inflation is affecting more than Thanksgiving staples like turkey or stuffing. Food prices on average have jumped around 24% over the last five years, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Some items have seen even sharper increases: Coffee and ground beef, for example, have each climbed by more than 40% in the same period despite pulling back from recent highs.
At the same time, millions of Americans lost SNAP benefits under policy changes included in President Donald Trump 's "big beautiful bill." Food banks across the U.S. have seen foot traffic skyrocket this year as the reduction in federal nutrition aid coincides with rising prices in grocery aisles.
The Salvation Army said some of its food pantries in October provided double or triple the amount of groceries than they did in the same month a year ago. Demand is now so high that some food banks in Feeding America's national network are worried about running out of supplies.
"We want to make sure that our food banks are as full as they possibly can be going into the holiday season," said Linda Nageotte, Feeding America's president and operations chief. "Far too many of them have empty shelves."
High energy prices as a result of the war with Iran are also affecting Americans' holiday plans.
Slightly fewer Americans will travel at least 50 miles around the Thanksgiving holiday in 2026, marking the first year-over-year decline since the country was in lockdown from the pandemic in 2020, according to AAA. Stacey Barber, a vice president at the auto association, attributed this year's pullback in part to higher fuel costs.
AAA said that about nine out of every 10 Thanksgiving travelers will do so by car. While gas prices have come down from a May peak, they are still up about 18% year over year and could set a new record for the month of November, according to the organization's data.
Travelers are paying about 31% and 23% more for roundtrip domestic airfare around Thanksgiving and Christmas, respectively, than they did a year ago, according to booking platform Hopper. Airlines have blamed the ticket price hikes on rising jet fuel costs in the wake of the war.
"There will be a significant shell shock when they see the price of traveling," said Hayley Berg, lead economist at Hopper.
Berg said price increases would feel more noticeable on routes previously serviced by Spirit, the budget airline that shut down in May. Travelers are booking holiday flights earlier than they did in past years, a sign that prices are top of mind, she said.
Staying home for the holidays isn't a silver-bullet solution, either, as heating costs jump.
The average American household is expected to spend 7% more on home heating this winter than they did last year, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association. For the typical family, that equates to an increase of about $66 and a total bill for the season above $1,000.
To be sure, some families will feel it more than others. Heating oil , which is used mainly in homes in the Northeast, has jumped around 70% year over year. However, natural gas , which is one of the most common heating types in the U.S., costs about the same as last year.
Some U.S. states, like Massachusetts and New York, beefed up their home energy support programs to account for higher prices. But Mark Wolfe, NEADA's executive director, said federal aid offerings haven't been meaningfully expanded this year.
"Some of these increases are caused directly by the decision to go to war," Wolfe said. "Why isn't the federal government helping families pay these higher bills?"
The spirit of giving will take on a different meaning for consumers this year.
Retail sales during the all-important holiday season are expected to grow almost 5% this year and surpass $1 trillion for the first time , according to Bain & Company. But the consulting firm said most of that growth would come from inflation, rather than from consumers buying more products.
And Citi on Wednesday said that increased holiday spending would be mainly driven by higher earners this year. The bank said that's a result of the "K"-shaped economy , a term used to describe a scenario where better-off Americans splash out while others struggle.
Toy prices have climbed more than 9% over the past year and now sit at their highest levels since 2019, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Manufacturers have raised prices in response to higher costs for transportation and plastic , according to Chris Byrne, an independent toy industry analyst. The artificial intelligence boom has driven up prices for the chips that power gaming devices and other electronics.
Byrne said that's causing shoppers to focus more on the quality of gifts rather than quantity.
"The toy industry always reflects the culture at large," Byrne said. "It's almost true economically as well. As inflation is rising, people are being a little bit more cautious about what they're buying."
Just 16% of respondents to a Morning Consult survey said they planned to spend more in the 2026 holiday season than they did a year ago. Respondents who were older or had lower earnings were more likely to say their budgets were shrinking, the survey found.
